topics.title: First words: people and places
topics.intro: Latin was the language of the Romans, and it is hiding inside half the words you already know. Start with fourteen words for people and places. Say each one aloud: Latin is pronounced as it is spelt, with “c” always hard as in “cat” and “v” said like “w”.
topics.teach: Teach three Latin words and the English words that come from them.
topics.talk: Ask her for the Latin for dog, and what “canine” means.
topics.hook: Latin hides inside English: **aqua** → aquarium, **villa** → village.

topics.title: Verbs: what people are doing
topics.intro: Latin verbs end in -t when they mean “he”, “she” or “it” does something: laborat means “he works” or “she works”. No separate word for “he” is needed.
topics.teach: Explain how you can tell a Latin verb means “he” or “she” does something.
topics.talk: Ask her what ambulat, dormit and clamat mean, then where “ambulance” comes from.
topics.hook: A Latin verb ending in **-t** means he or she is doing it: **amat**, he or she loves.

topics.title: Reading simple sentences
topics.intro: Latin usually puts the verb LAST: “servus laborat” is “the slave works”. Latin has no words for “the” or “a”, so you add them in English.
topics.teach: Translate “puella in horto sedet” and explain the word order.
topics.talk: Make up a three-word Latin sentence together.
topics.hook: Find the verb first: Latin usually saves it for the end of the sentence.

topics.title: Who does what: nominative and accusative
topics.intro: In Latin the ENDING tells you who is doing the action and who it is done to. “servus puellam videt”: the slave (servus) sees the girl (puellam). Swap the endings and the girl sees the slave, whatever the word order.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between puella and puellam.
topics.talk: “canis puerum videt” or “canem puer videt”: who sees whom? (Same answer both times!)
topics.hook: The **-m** marks who is on the receiving end: puella**m** is the girl as the object.

topics.title: I, you, he: verb endings
topics.intro: Change the ending, change the person: ambulo (I walk), ambulas (you walk), ambulat (he or she walks). The verb “to be” is irregular, just like in English: sum, es, est.
topics.teach: Explain what -o, -s and -t tell you at the end of a Latin verb.
topics.talk: Ask her to say “I sleep”, “you sleep” and “she sleeps” in Latin.
topics.hook: Chant the endings: **-o, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt** (I, you, he or she, we, you all, they).

topics.title: More than one: -ae, -i, -nt
topics.intro: One girl is puella; two girls are puellae. One slave is servus; several are servi. When the subject is plural, the verb ends -nt: servi laborant.
topics.teach: Explain how to make puella and servus plural, and what happens to the verb.
topics.talk: Ask her the Latin for “the dogs are sleeping” (canes dormiunt is 3rd declension; try “servi dormiunt”).
topics.hook: More than one: **-ae** and **-i** for the people, **-nt** on the verb: puellae ambulant.

topics.title: More words: food, home and the city
topics.intro: Fourteen more words, this time for food, the home and the city. Watch for the English words hiding inside them.
topics.teach: Teach three words from this set with their English relatives.
topics.talk: At dinner: ask her the Latin for food, water and table.
topics.hook: Home and food words live on in English: **domus** → domestic, **panis** → pantry.

topics.title: Numbers and greetings
topics.intro: Counting to ten in Latin explains the names of four months and dozens of English words. Plus five phrases to greet a Roman politely.
topics.teach: Count to ten in Latin and explain why September is not the seventh month.
topics.talk: Greet each other in Latin for a day: salve in the morning, vale at bedtime.
topics.hook: **Unus, duo, tres**: a unicycle has one wheel, a duet has two singers, a triangle three corners.

topics.title: Latin inside English
topics.intro: About half of English vocabulary comes from Latin, often through French. Knowing the Latin root lets you work out words you have never seen.
topics.teach: Pick an English word, find the Latin inside it, and explain how the meaning connects.
topics.talk: Spot three Latin-rooted words on a cereal box or in the news.
topics.hook: Spot the root: **port** = carry (porter, transport), **scrib** = write (scribble, script).

topics.title: Roman life
topics.intro: The words tell you how the Romans lived: a house with an open-roofed hall, dinner lying down, school with a wax tablet, and numbers you still see on clock faces.
topics.teach: Describe a Roman house using the Latin names of its rooms.
topics.talk: Find Roman numerals on a clock, a film’s end credits or a building.
topics.hook: The Romans gave us straight roads, public baths, and July and August (after Julius Caesar and Augustus).

topics.title: A short story: the family at home
topics.intro: A whole story in Latin, using only words you know. Read it twice, aloud if you can, then answer the questions.
topics.talk: Ask her to read the story aloud to you, then translate a sentence of your choice.
topics.hook: Read Latin in chunks: find the verb at the end, then look for **-m** to see who it happens to.

items.explain: “Felix in culina cenam parat.” Felix is the servus (slave) and the cook.
items.passage:
Marcus est pater. Iulia est mater. Lucius est filius. Flavia est filia.
Marcus in horto sedet. Iulia in atrio laborat. Felix est servus. Felix in culina cenam parat.
Rufus est canis. Rufus in via dormit. Lucius canem videt. Lucius clamat: “Rufe!” Rufus ad Lucium currit.
Flavia aquam portat. Felix cenam portat. familia in triclinio cenat. Rufus sub mensa dormit.
items.passageSource: A short story written for this app
